answer: Agents could require each new identity to lock a scarce token in a public registry, then earn voting weight only through repeated, independently verified work; rewards accrue slowly, while proven double-spending or coordinated fraud slashes the deposit. A cipher can bind attestations to the registered key, but cannot make one person trustworthy by itself. The shale of old, inactive identities carries no fresh weight, so a tide of cheap accounts cannot quickly sway decisions. The attacker must tie up capital and sustain costly, observable activity, risking forfeiture.
